procedural_history.originating_court: Ld. XIV Metropolitan Magistrate, Egmore, Chennai (Trial Court)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 24.10.2019 passed by the Trial Court rejecting the application instituted by the Complainant under Section 216 read with Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (the “CrPC”) seeking (i) the summoning of; and (ii) the impleadment of the Appellant(s) as accused person(s) in connection with Case Crime No. 7243 of 2018 under Section(s) 452, 294(b), 323 and 506(1) of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (the “IPC”).
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Revision petitions were filed by Appellant No. 1 and Respondent No.2 before the Madras High Court against the Trial Court's order. The High Court allowed the revision petitions on 10.06.2019, setting aside the Trial Court's order and remanding the application back to the Trial Court for reconsideration, because the Appellants were not issued notice in the Underlying Application.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellants appealed to the Supreme Court assailing the correctness of the Madras High Court's decision dated 13.09.2021. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the High Court's order.

directions: The Impugned Order is set aside.
Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the order passed by the trial court whereunder, the trial court rejected the application filed by the complainant u/s. 216/319 CrPC seeking the summoning of, and the impleadment of the appellants as accused persons in connection with the case u/ss. 452, 294(b), 323 and 506(1) IPC.

facts: The complainant filed an application before the trial court under Sections 216/319 of the CrPC to summon and implead the appellants as accused persons in a criminal case.
The trial court considered the application and rejected it.
The complainant challenged this rejection before the High Court.

The High Court set aside the trial court's order, holding that there was a prima facie case against the appellants based on the complaint and witness statements, and directed the trial court to implead them as accused.
law: The discretionary power under Section 319 of the CrPC, which allows a court to proceed against other persons appearing to be guilty of an offence, must be used sparingly and only when circumstances warrant it.
The standard of evidence required to invoke Section 319 is higher than a prima facie case (the standard used for framing charges).
The correct threshold is evidence that is "more than a prima facie case... but short of evidence that if left unrebutted would lead to conviction."
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had applied the wrong legal standard. The High Court impleaded the appellants based on a mere "prima-facie finding," which is an insufficient threshold for exercising power under Section 319 CrPC.
The Supreme Court held that the trial court's original order rejecting the application was "well reasoned and did not suffer from any perversity."

It concluded that the materials on record, which included vague allegations and witness statements, did not meet the high evidentiary threshold required to summon additional accused under Section 319 CrPC.
The High Court failed to appreciate that this power should be used sparingly.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's decision, concluding that the High Court was not justified in setting aside the trial court's order. The High Court had erroneously applied a lower 'prima facie' standard instead of the higher evidentiary threshold required for Section 319 CrPC. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the order passed by the trial court whereunder, the trial court rejected the application filed by the complainant u/s. 216/319 CrPC seeking the summoning of, and the impleadment of the appellants as accused persons in connection with the case u/ss. 452, 294(b), 323 and 506(1) IPC.
appellant_arguments: The High Court erroneously exercised its jurisdiction under Section 319 of the CrPC to reverse the Trial Court's order.
The High Court failed to appreciate that the allegations against the appellants are vague and omnibus.
There is no evidence on record to suggest the involvement of the appellants in the alleged offence.
The High Court did not properly apply the legal principles laid down by the Supreme Court in Hardeep Singh v State of Punjab & Ors.
respondent_arguments: The High Court rightly appreciated the allegations in the complaint, the statements recorded under Section 161 CrPC, and the examination-in-chief of the prosecution witnesses.
The evidence on record clearly showed the involvement of the appellants in the commission of the crime.
The High Court's order was not perverse and was justified in view of the decision in Jitendra Nath Mishra v. State of Uttar Pradesh.

cases.case_name: Hardeep Singh v State of Punjab & Ors.
cases.principle: The power under Section 319 of the CrPC is a discretionary and extraordinary power which should be exercised sparingly, and the test for its application is one which is more than a prima facie case as exercised at the time of framing of charge, but short of satisfaction to an extent that the evidence, if it goes unrebutted, would lead to conviction.

cases.case_name: Sagar v. State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
cases.principle: Reiterated the position that the discretionary power under Section 319 CrPC ought to be used sparingly and only where the circumstances of the case so warrant, satisfying a threshold that is more than a prima facie case.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The discretionary and extraordinary power under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure must be exercised sparingly, and only when the evidence on record meets a standard that is more than a prima facie case required for framing a charge, but short of the satisfaction that the evidence, if left unrebutted, would lead to a conviction.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court erred in setting aside the Trial Court's order because it applied the wrong legal standard. The High Court impleaded the appellants based on a mere prima-facie finding, whereas the correct test for invoking the extraordinary power under Section 319 CrPC requires a higher threshold of evidence: more than a prima facie case as used for framing charges, but just short of evidence that would lead to a conviction if unrebutted. The materials on record did not meet this higher standard, and the Trial Court's original order was well-reasoned and not perverse.
legal_tests_applied: The crucial test for invoking power under Section 319 of the CrPC is one which is more than a prima facie case as exercised at the time of framing of charge, but short of satisfaction to an extent that the evidence, if it goes unrebutted, would lead to conviction.
why_respondent_won: The High Court failed to appreciate that the discretionary powers under Section 319 CrPC ought to have been used sparingly where circumstances of the case so warrant.
The High Court impleaded the appellants as accused persons on the satisfaction of a prima-facie finding, which is an incorrect and lower standard than what is required by law.

The materials on record could not be said to have satisfied the required threshold, which is more than a prima facie case as exercised at the time of framing of charge but short of evidence that if left unrebutted would lead to conviction.
The Trial Court's original order was well reasoned and did not suffer from any perversity, and therefore should not have been set aside.
policy_considerations: The power Under Section 319 of the Code is a discretionary and extraordinary power which should be exercised sparingly and only in those cases where the circumstances of the case so warrant.
